newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foreign crudes trickle in, Iraq deals pending.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foreign crudes trickle in, Iraq deals pending.

text.p: Foreign crudes trickled into the U.S. Gulf Coast on Wednesday as refiners moved to cement the first supply contracts with Iraq in six years, traders said.
The spread between January West Texas Intermediate and North Sea Brent hovered around $1.15-20 a barrel.
Trans-Atlantic arbitrage opportunities remain limited, although one Wall Street player sold a Brent VLCC for loading December 21 to a Gulf Coast refiner at an unspecified price, traders said.
Another Wall Streeter apparently failed to sell a separate VLCC for loading December 25, and is eyeing storage options in the Caribbean, they added.

Elsewhere, a "semi-distressed" cargo of sweet Canadian Rainbow crude was sold on the Gulf Coast amid tight pipeline conditions in Canada. Rainbow was last sold on the Gulf Coast at West Texas Intermediate plus 10-20 cents, trade sources said.
Coastal, meanwhile, was the first U.S. company to ink a contract with Iraq under the U.N.-sponsored oil-for-food deal.
Coastal's contract for 60,000 barrels per day is pending final U.N. approval, the sources said.

Iraqi crude is attracting interest in South America as well. Petrobras is negotiating with Iraqi State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) to buy 20,000 to 30,000 bpd of Iraqi crude, a Petrobras official said.
Before Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, Brazil imported a peak of 300,000 bpd of Iraqi Kirkuk and Basrah Light grades on a term and spot basis, the official said.
In the U.S. aftermarket, a Wall Street firm bought a series of partial paper January Brent cargoes at between $22.25 and $22.30 a barrel, nine to 14 cents higher than the IPE settlement price.
Intermonth spreads were weaker, with Jan/Feb Brent changing hands at 44/45 cents, compared to 52 cents at the London close.
